summary:
Private consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults has been lawful in Guatemala since 1871.

Guatemala provides no legal gender recognition for trans people. Since 2016 a person may change a legal name to match gender identity only with judicial permission. Legal gender cannot be changed. A person cannot self-report gender for official documents, which must show the sex and name assigned at birth. The resulting mismatch between appearance and identity documents exposes trans visitors to scrutiny during identity checks.

Guatemala is bound by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018, OC-24/17, which holds that recognition of gender identity on official documents is a human right under the American Convention on Human Rights and which requires access to marriage and all existing family registration systems for same-sex couples. Guatemala was among the countries urged in January 2018 to comply. Compliance has not been recorded.

A December 2017 bill that would have recognized the right to gender identity and permitted change of name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by the Legislative and Constitutional Points Commission and the Women's Commission. A later proposal for a gender identity law to allow correction of official documents was advocated but was not enacted. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2022 on legislative attacks including bills that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

Vociferous opposition defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash against legal gender recognition in Guatemala.

Guatemalan law prohibits no discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations including cafes, restaurants, nightclubs and cinemas. A May 2017 bill to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category was not adopted.

No hate-crime protection covers gender identity. Bias-motivated crimes on that basis are reported to be tolerated by the Government, particularly harassment and violence directed at transgender people. The lack of protection is attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles.

Guatemalan officials have excluded trans women from femicide protections on the stated ground that transgender women are not biological women. Central American governments have long maintained that exclusion. The exclusion is official and shapes the violence risk for trans women in Guatemala.

Trans women held in custody are placed according to birth sex in the men's prison system, a practice documented as of 2020. Placement in men's prisons facilitates anti-trans violence and exposes trans women to sexual assault. Trans activist Barbara Herrarte of Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans described repeated forced sex at night by other detainees while held in a men's prison.

United Nations and non-governmental reports from the late 1990s documented systematic lethal targeting of LGBT people as part of a social cleansing campaign. That record includes the 1997 shooting in Guatemala City of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia.

Guatemala grants no legal recognition to same-sex couples through marriage, civil unions or domestic partnership. A civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by Deputy Sandra Moran has not been debated since. Lawmakers responded to the Inter-American Court opinion with Initiative 5272, the Protection of Life and Family Act, to explicitly ban same-sex marriage, define family as a father, a mother and children, increase penalties for abortion, provide that freedom of conscience and expression protects refusal to accept non-heterosexual conduct as normal, and describe homosexuality as contrary to biology and genetics. The initiative passed first and second readings but its third reading was blocked in September 2018 with no debate since. A renewed congressional approval of Law 5272 on 9 March 2022 to ban same-sex marriage and punish abortion with 5 years in prison was archived and discarded on 15 March after President Alejandro Giammattei announced a veto as violating the Constitution and international agreements.

Bill 5490 advanced in December 2021 to remove education regarding transgender people from schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents from gender identity disorders and to require censorship of media including transgender people. The Education, Science and Technology Committee of Congress approved it unanimously and sent it for full congressional review.
tangentialFactors:
Guatemalan law also prohibits no discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations. The 1997 Code on Childhood and Youth had safeguarded children and youth from discrimination based on their own or parental sexual orientation but was repealed in 2003. A May 2017 bill to add sexual orientation to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 was not adopted.

The Inter-American Court opinion advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, with backlash reported in all four countries. That regional context helps explain non-implementation in Guatemala.

Openly LGBT representation entered Congress with lesbian Deputy Sandra Moran elected in January 2016 and gay Deputy Aldo Davila elected in June 2019 on a platform to criminalize hate crimes and hate speech against LGBT people. Former President Alvaro Colom supported civil unions. President Jimmy Morales supported the ban proposal and stated that Guatemala believes in family based on marriage between a man and a woman. Most residents adhere to Catholic, Fundamentalist Pentecostal or Eastern Orthodox faiths, whose socially conservative teachings on homosexuality and cross-dressing are reflected in dominant political parties, while most other parties ignore LGBT rights.
localsOnly:
Mismatch between gender identity and mandatory birth-assigned documents causes problems for residents in accessing government services including education and basic resources that require official identification.

Lambda, an LGBTQ organization, flags forced internal displacement from violence.

Active Evangelical-funded conversion therapy centers, mainly in rural areas, subject persons to electroshock therapy, forced marriage, coerced sex and corrective rape that is prosecuted only as rape and not as a hate crime.
outOfScopeNotes:
Guatemala's compliance with OC-24/17 on marriage equality and legal gender recognition is not sourced beyond the 2018 call to comply and the subsequent rejected and unadopted bills.

The content and current status of the later advocated gender identity law proposal is not sourced beyond advocacy without enactment.

The outcome of Bill 5490 after committee approval and referral for full congressional review is not sourced.

No gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on trans custody were recorded as of the 2020 prison report. Current placement practice beyond that date is unresolved.

Whether corrective rape, forced marriage and other conversion practices documented in centers were directed specifically at trans persons as distinct from lesbian, gay and bisexual persons is not sourced in disaggregated form.
